newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN takes no action on ending Serbia sanctions.
newsitem.headline: UN takes no action on ending Serbia sanctions.

text.p: The Security Council on Tuesday did not end sanctions against the rump Yugoslav state as Russia had wanted although diplomats said they expected Washington and Moscow to agree on a solution shortly.

Russia's ambassador Sergei Lavrov had drawn up a document that would end the sanctions on Tuesday but the United States rejected it, saying the September 14 Bosnian elections had not been certified yet.
At a closed door council meeting, diplomats said China felt the sanctions should be lifted immediately.

And other members were said to have warned the council not to include other factors in a sanctions-lifting resolution, a reference to Russia's proposal that Yugoslavia's suspension to the General Assembly and other U.N. bodies end at the same time. The United States opposes this.

Sanctions against the Yugoslav state of Serbia and Montegraro were suspended by the council last November as a follow up to the U.S.-initiated Balkan peace accords signed in Dayton, Ohio last year. The council's resolution stipulated the sanctions would be lifted entirely 10 days after the Bosnian elections, which to Moscow meant Sept. 24.

But the United States has interpreted the resolution as saying the 10-day countdown should begin after the the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), has certified the elections in writing.
Asked where Britain stood in the controversy, Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind told reporters the issue was still under discussion and the question was "a technical one."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Monday that "the United States is very clear that the 10-day period refers to the period after certification by the OSCE and that has not happened yet."

The United States has said previously it would keep a so-called outer ring of sanctions, such as preventing the rump Yugoslav state of Serbia and Montenegro from institutions like the International Monetary Fund.
Rifkind said western European statess agreed and have linked Yugoslavia's re-entry to financial institutions to progress on the restive Serbian province of Kosovo, dominated by ethnic Albanians.
"We all believe there has to be leverage," he said.

In addition the United States was considering inserting into a resolution a threat of imposing sanctions in the future should the Dayton accords be violated. But it is highly improbable the council would agree to re-impose the bans.

Momcilo Krajisnik, the Bosnian Serb representative in the newly-elected Bosnian presidency and an outspoken advocate of Serb secession, has refused to travel to Sarajevo for an initial meeting of the three-member state presidency.
This new body would be chaired by Moslem President Alija Izetbegovic who won the most votes and include Kremiri Zuban, the Croat representative,
Discussions on a resolution are taking place mainly in an expanded so-called contact group on the Balkans that includes the United States, Russia, Britain, France, Germany and Italy.
